#9039. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

#9038. Five Questions for Advisors on the November Marquee Sales: Guarantees, Spotty Bidding, and a $190 M. Van Gogh

By Harrison Jacobs, Daniel Cassady, Brian Boucher November 25, 2026 11:00am

Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance, the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday.

It’s Thanksgiving week and, for those of us who live and breathe the art market, that means only the briefest of breaks between the all-important November auction season and the year’s grand finale at Art Basel Miami Beach. But before we turn to Miami, a quick post-mortem on the marquee sales just passed.

Perhaps more than in any other industry, the health of the art market is in the eye of the beholder. Do you measure it by overall totals? By sell-through rate? By the number of bidders, or the number of guaranteed lots? By the ratio of hammer prices to estimates? Each figure tells a slightly different story, leaving plenty for our resident market whisperers to debate. But before we turn this week’s column over to the advisers, let’s set out some basic figures.

According to data from ARTDAI, the November evening sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips generated $2.03 billion, a modest 7.5 percent increase over 2025, but the highest total since 2022. Sotheby’s led the pack with $1.16 billion, clearing $1 billion and taking more than half of the three houses’ combined total for the second straight year. (Its share rose to 57 percent from 53 percent. Christie’s share dropped to 38 percent from 43 percent, while Phillips’s ticked up to 5 percent from 4 percent, pushed by the $44.6 million Modigliani sculpture.)

And yes, the $384 million gap between Sotheby’s and Christie’s is roughly what the Blaquier-Arrieta collection brought in on its own: $412 million on just 12 lots. Winning those big consignments really does matter.

But for all those gaudy totals, there was a definite sense watching the week’s sales that bidding was uneven, thin, and at times absent entirely. Blame fickle collectors, sure, but it seems the auction houses pushed their estimates to the limit. Per ARTDAI, hammer prices across the various-owner sales in November 2025 came in 17 percent above the low estimates and at roughly 80 percent of the high estimates. This season, hammer prices for the same sales (i.e. excluding the Blaquier-Arrieta single-owner sale) were flat against the low estimates and just 69 percent of the highs. As Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart said after the Blaquier-Arrieta sale last week, “Our estimates weren’t shy.”

But does an aggressive auction house make for a weak market? Or is this the same market we’ve seen for the last few cycles—one that is choosy, blue-chip and provenance-driven, and competitive for the right objects—just approached differently by the specialists? That’s what we asked the advisers, along with their takes on everything from the spread of guarantees to that $190 million van Gogh.

Answers have been edited for clarity and concision.

Evan Beard, Beard & Co: Our having to repeatedly chase Impressionist and Modern Day Sale works well above the high estimates with a fairly low hit rate tells us that the “flight to safety” is more than just a tired cliché. Even second- and third-tier Impressionists performed very well.

Liz Sterling, Sterling | Teel Capital: The strong result for the Jeff Koons Bob-Tail [at Sotheby’s] was a pleasant reminder that no matter how highly orchestrated evening sales have become, there are still surprises. Equally, the results for the small Robert Ryman and Robert Rauschenberg from the Agnes Gund collection clearly demonstrate that there is still connoisseurship in the market.

Nina del Rio, del Rio | Byers: I have always believed the market is driven by the number of participants; more bidders = higher prices, more volatility, and less predictability. The current moment feels more predictable, safe, and tempered—which would signal fewer bidders. Estimates were full, reflecting strong performance over the past few seasons, and the buyers are still there for the majority of material, which is European Impressionism and modernism and American postwar abstraction, but there was less competition and flatter prices as a result.

However, I was surprised by the sober bidding on the truly rare material, which represented a singular (once-in-a-lifetime) opportunity for buyers. Monday evening after the Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary auction, I told ARTnews I was excited for the Blaquier sale on Wednesday because of the rarity and quality of the works; well, I was wrong that rarity would translate into bidder competition and runaway prices. The fact is, each work was priced at the top end of the artists’ (very mature) markets—leaving little room for price discovery, and bidding was thin and tempered as a result. Did buyers perceive these prices as the very top end of the market? Yes, I think so, which meant little to no competition for great works.

Maria Brito: Believe it or not, the moment that caught my attention happened in Stockholm, with the sale of Hilma af Klint’s Ser III No. 5. It hammered at 108 million Swedish kronor against a high estimate of 8 million, an extraordinary 13.5 times the estimate! Here is an artist whose importance to the history of abstraction has been celebrated by major museums for years, but whose market barely existed because so few of her abstract paintings ever became available. And suddenly collectors were fighting to pay nearly $13 million for one.

We saw something similar with Aaron Douglas’s Harriet Tubman in New York, which sparked a seven-minute bidding war involving eight bidders and sold for $14.48 million against a high estimate of $3.5 million. I think this tells us something fascinating about today’s market. There is enormous capital available for historically significant, genuinely rare works, particularly by artists whose contributions have been undervalued. Collectors are willing to reconsider established price hierarchies, and when they really want something, they’re not shy about spending.

Allan Schwartzman, Schwartzman&: For me, there were several standout points: the fever for hot young artists at auction has passed; Robert Rauschenberg remains the most important innovator of the last 75 years, and yet his market remains undeservedly quiet; and behind that, Gilbert & George are a crazy bargain; even though their work is photographic, they are unique and should be commanding the prices of the great painters of their generation.

Erica Samuels, Samuels Creative: Beyond prices, this week highlighted a distinct mood across the field. There is a strong sense of collegiality—advisors, dealers, and auction houses are actively working together to ensure success for their clients amid a generally sideways market. The market relies as much on goodwill as it does on capital, and both were evident this week. Despite broader tech and financial shifts, such as the Anthropic IPO, this remains a human-driven market centered on human-made art.

Danielle Forest Brandi, Beaumont Nathan: There were a few revealing moments for us, but among them was the spectacular result for Monet’s La Barque. The price of $6.9 million was, on the one hand, a surprising result for a work that measured only 2 by 3 inches, but on the other hand, a good case study for how collectors are behaving at the top end of the market. Looking at that alone, it’s perhaps an irrational result, but when you think about the rarity of the object, the story, and how good that picture will look on someone’s wall, i.e., styled alongside their Chinese porcelain collection and Nakashima furniture, it starts to make sense. That’s how collectors are thinking right now; it’s the beauty of the art market and what makes collecting different from other pursuits.

Evan Beard: Two key themes drove the high third-party guarantee rate this season: (1) Much of the material came from single-owner sales that carried house guarantees—Blaquier, Baum, Clive Davis, etc.—so the houses had to put the risk off on third parties. (2) Consignor expectations were elevated coming off a strong spring season, which pushed estimates to a level that the houses felt more comfortable locking in guarantees rather than risk a lot going unsold.

Guarantees are fundamental at this point. They’re a behavior tool to get an early bid from a buyer and a behavioral tool to give comfort to a consignor. Both sides still have the chance at upside. Guarantees are an important lubricant.

Nina del Rio: Estimates were high across both auction houses, reflecting the past six years of consistent demand and solid performance—especially for European modernism and postwar American abstraction. The auction houses agree to full estimates to compete for consignments. My guess is that Christie’s was less willing to offer house guarantees which were not backed by irrevocable bids at the start of the consignment-getting season. And Sotheby’s had a bit more faith that they would find an IB [irrevocable bid] later in the process. In brief, I believe Sotheby’s appetite for risk—and possibly their confidence in the market—was a bit stronger this season.

Maria Brito: Sotheby’s just announced its biggest-ever week of fine art sales at $1.31 billion, which is extraordinary. But let’s look underneath those numbers. Almost a third of that total came from just 12 paintings in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, all guaranteed, and the majority hammered below their low estimates. Sotheby’s guaranteed 77 percent of its evening lots compared with 47 percent at Christie’s, suggesting a much more aggressive approach to securing major consignments. Guarantees are essential to attracting exceptional property, and third-party guarantors can absorb much of the risk. But a guaranteed sale tells us little about competitive demand. What interests me is how many collectors were willing to bid beyond the guaranteed price. The money is clearly there. The willingness to compete at any price is another matter.

Allan Schwartzman: The numbers speak for themselves; I don’t have any great insights here.

Erica Samuels: Each house has a different appetite for risk and adapts its strategy based on the specific estate or group of works. So I think comparing things side by side is tricky because it’s not apples to apples. While guaranteeing lots significantly affects outcome variations, there is clear demand right now for artists like Warhol (Flowers, Soup Can), Celmins, and Albers in postwar, as well as Tanguy, Kandinsky, and Monet in the modern.

Danielle Forest Brandi: The IB market is relatively saturated at the moment, and there is a lot of competition. To be in the game, you need to be quick, decisive, and on the inside track. Collectors are clearly enjoying the ability to gain a competitive advantage through the IB mechanism, and it shapes behavior enormously. We find that collectors who don’t get the IB early on may not bid without it. That said, this season showed us that when the guarantees are set too high, it can take the energy out of the room and make it harder for works to inspire competitive bidding.

Evan Beard: Elevated estimates repel potential bids. Blaquier estimates crowded out potential bids. Most works get auctioned three times in a season: the auction between the houses for the material; the auction among potential guarantors; and, finally, the auction among the general public. The first two auctions erode the margin for the houses. Keeping estimates low while winning consignments is always a tricky dance.

Liz Sterling: I think a lot of works found their market this season regardless of where the presale estimate was set. Where presale estimates were overly aggressive, the auction houses worked hard to match reserves to bids and get works sold. Conversely, works that were conservatively estimated, such as the Aaron Douglas and Edward Hopper at Sotheby’s, saw competition and achieved prices well in excess of their presale estimates.

Nina del Rio: The markets for the high-profile works this season, which were largely European Impressionist and modern, and American Abstract Expressionist, are all relatively mature, and the top end of the artists’ prices have largely been realized. Couple this with full estimates (which the auction houses had to offer sellers to win the business) and it leaves little room for price discovery, even for the exceedingly rare Blaquier van Gogh. I believe this affected competition for the van Gogh, the entire Blaquier sale, and several other highlights across all the auction houses. However, I can’t help but wonder whether the last-minute claim on the van Gogh took other bidders out of the mix? Just a thought … and certainly not unique to me.

Maria Brito: I think we’re reading too much into the number of bidders. In 2022, when the global art market reached its second-highest level in history, Orchard with Cypresses from the Paul Allen collection sold for $117.2 million with exactly three bidders. This week’s van Gogh also attracted three bidders, but fetched $190.4 million, more than 60 percent above the previous record. I consider Châtaigniers en fleurs a substantially better painting. Yes, it hammered at $165 million, below Sotheby’s $180 million expectation, but that doesn’t make the result disappointing. We also cannot ignore the Nazi-era provenance controversy, settled barely a day before the auction. Whether it deterred potential bidders is impossible to know. At this level of the market, buyers have extraordinary financial resources, but they still have their own ideas about value.

Allan Schwartzman: It brought a huge price. There were few bids because the auction houses sometimes have to stretch to get headline material. Many works that are competitively offered sell on few bids because the auction houses have already conducted an auction between themselves to get those works. This does not necessarily reflect a thin market.

Erica Samuels: I enjoy the philosophical roundabout of auction house estimates. There are different categories: the attractive, come-hither estimate; the punchy estimate; the estimate right in line with the market. It’s pretty nuanced, and you have to be careful about reading too much into them. An estimate is not a price tag. It’s a range, a suggestion. And to a certain extent, there’s a part of the auction world you only understand if you’re out there seeing a lot of things. Some artworks couldn’t sell privately, so they come to auction to try a broader audience. They may not find a buyer at any estimate.

But let’s be honest, it’s quite thin at the top. $190 million is a lot of money for any buyer to spend. No wonder it sold to a very seasoned professional.

Danielle Forest Brandi: The discrepancy between headline prices and estimates was a defining feature of the week. In recent years, the houses drove down estimates in an effort to revive competition, but it seems that pricing has crept back up. The thinness we saw with bidding was more indicative of these ambitious estimates than the market overall.

Evan Beard: From 2020 to 2023, we were in a pretty intense risk-on speculation cycle where emerging contemporary was hot, so a lot of that material got flipped to auction. We’re in a risk-off cycle now. So very few emerging contemporary lots need to go to auction because they are easily accessible privately. The pendulum will swing back, albeit for a new group of hot young artists.

Nina del Rio: There was a lot of American postwar and contemporary material on the market last week, but few really great, major examples in the auctions. Rothko, de Kooning, Richter, Frankenthaler, and Stella (among others) were well represented with fully priced seven- and eight-figure examples, but nothing outstanding or market-making vs. the great European material on offer. (It is worth noting that women artists from the same postwar period performed better, but were still uneven—Kusama and Agnes Martin in particular.)

De Kooning and Rothko are interesting case studies. While de Kooning was well represented, especially by the 1975 oil from the Hedreen collection at Sotheby’s and the Whitney’s de Kooning at Christie’s, both were fully estimated, and neither had the potential to push the artist’s market. Four Rothko paintings on paper were offered last week; one very good example sold well above estimate, and the other three examples, which were arguably not as strong, sold below estimate or were unsold.

Maria Brito: The contemporary market is suffering from serious fatigue. There are simply too many artists, too much work being produced, and too much material circulating. Collectors have become desensitized and increasingly skeptical, particularly after watching so many artists’ prices rise dramatically and then collapse.

Compare that with Impressionism and modern art, where the universe of historically established artists is considerably smaller and the supply of important works is finite. There’s a level of scarcity and historical validation that gives buyers confidence. Contemporary art is a much more crowded field, and there’s simply not enough demand to support everyone at the prices we’ve become accustomed to seeing.

Of course, exceptional artists and exceptional works will continue to command extraordinary prices, but collectors are increasingly questioning what’s genuinely worth pursuing. And I think that’s healthy.

Allan Schwartzman: The fever for hot young artists at auction is over for now. This is for several reasons: prices for most young artists for whom there was hysterical (read: speculative) buying at auction could not and did not live up to such lofty numbers; a new generation of artists has not emerged for which the market has the same speculative appetite (and that’s a good thing); and sometimes the market for young artists is very different at auction than at the galleries that represent artists and develop those markets.

Erica Samuels: Collectors are looking for historical depth far more than in previous seasons. A new wave of younger collectors is definitely entering the market. They are educated, critical thinkers who ask great questions, which makes for an exciting path forward. They want collections that move across generations of artists, not just one moment.

Danielle Forest Brandi: With some exceptions, the contemporary offering across both houses this season felt a bit tired in [the] view [of myself and my colleagues at Beaumont Nathan], especially in comparison to the Impressionist and modern. The depth and cultural authority of blue-chip modernism seems to offer an assuring sense of solidity and substance that is perhaps universally needed right now. Of course, tastes change, the market moves on, and in time the contemporary world will come back as that market continues to recalibrate. But in the meantime, it seems to us that collectors are more interested in the past than the present.

Evan Beard: Anyone who tells you that Gen Z is driving the art market in any meaningful way is either misinformed or trying to sell you a dream. The market is driven by a group of private equity, hedge fund, real estate, and tech entrepreneurs in their 50s and 60s. It’s the usual suspects. And each new year a few new big buyers enter the fray. New wealth grows up and ultimately buys art. But young collectors are not a major driver at auction at the moment. How many Gen Z collectors are on the ARTnews Top 200 collectors list? Or the Forbes 400 list? Or any list? Their day is coming, though. We’ve got some young risers we’re working with.

Nina del Rio: I would be guessing if I had an answer to this question. Here’s what I know: buyer access to great quality primary market material, while still difficult and often reserved for museums, is less difficult than in the past. I believe the younger collectors are buying great material from galleries (as they should). There is less great material by living artists at auction, and the speculation in that auction market has quieted considerably.

Maria Brito: I didn’t see clear evidence of a major generational shift this week, but the reality is that we rarely know who the ultimate buyers are. So much of the bidding happens through advisors, dealers, and telephone representatives. The auction houses know who’s behind those paddles. The rest of us are largely guessing. There’s certainly growing participation from younger collectors, but we should distinguish between buying a $20,000 print and bidding $100 million on a painting. Younger wealth is entering the market, but I haven’t seen compelling evidence from this week’s sales that it has fundamentally changed who’s buying at the very top.

Allan Schwartzman: I was not in the room to observe live bidding.

Danielle Forest Brandi: Impressionism was clearly the dominant category during the November sales, across different levels of the market. We are seeing a growing generation of collectors who are engaged with this area and other historical categories, seeking established blue-chip names or, the inverse, overlooked artists in history like the female Surrealists. Prices across many historical areas of the market have come down from where they once were, making accessible entry points for newer collectors who want to buy things that have substance and will hold up over time.

#9037. Comment | A missed opportunity for a full accounting of cultural cleansing

An installation view of Heritage in Resistance: Timbuktu to Odessa, at the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine in Paris, until 3 January 2027 Photo: © Didier Plowy

It is always gratifying to see one’s work referenced—especially 20 years after the fact. The exhibition Heritage in Resistance: Timbuktu to Odessa, at the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine in Paris (until 3 January 2027), traces attacks on material and intangible culture in conflicts beginning with the dynamiting of the Bamiyan Buddhas in 2001 and ending in Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza.

The vast exhibition spans art, digital re-creations, photography and filmed interviews. It is conceived of as an investigative report organised into sections on erasure, resistance and repair.

A wall text references my 2006 book The Destruction of Memory: Architecture at War, which first set out systematically why such targeting happens. The exhibition credits me with coining the term “cultural cleansing” in respect of the Bosnian War to explain the pattern of heritage erasure that can accompany, or presage, ethnic cleansing and the persecution of populations. It notes that Unesco adopted the term from 2012 to describe “the destruction of World Heritage Sites by terrorist groups”.

Except that book says much more than that. It talked about this same process in other places such as the Israel-occupied West Bank. It examined cultural genocide (like cultural cleansing, this still has no definition in international law) witnessed in instances ranging from the Ottoman Empire and Native American populations to the Holocaust and Tibet. I would now add the experiences of the Uyghurs in China, the Rohingya in Myanmar, the Yazidis in Iraq and the Palestinians in Gaza to that dreadful list. I argue that patterns of heritage destruction can evidence genocidal intent. Other genocides, such as that in Rwanda, did not have a pronounced material culture component.

These are matters that the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine exhibition unacceptably skirts. As in Germany and the UK (where a talk at London’s Building Centre including Architects for Gaza was cancelled following an intervention by Lawyers for Israel this summer), the French state and its institutions are censoring pro-Palestinian voices.The crucial work of Forensic Architecture in documenting destruction, for example, is not present after a dispute over the group’s use of “the G word”. How can you explain what has happened to Gaza’s cultural heritage unless you are at least prepared to discuss possible intent and patterns of destruction?

As an investigative report, the show obfuscates as much as it reveals. Institutions and governments shield themselves behind the argument that it is up to the courts to determine genocide. They forget the Genocide Convention’s duties of prevention—as litigated in the 2007 International Court of Justice (ICJ) case, Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro, or South Africa’s inclusion of attacks on culture when considering Palestinian “conditions of life” at the ICJ.

An installation view of Heritage in Resistance: Timbuktu to Odessa, at the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine in Paris, until 3 January 2027 Photo: © Didier Plowy

There is an impression that heritage destruction in conflicts has got worse over recent decades and that the propaganda impact of destruction is actually exploited by some groups. The jury is out on this. As reflected in the show, however, the international heritage community has had an almost singular focus on actions by terrorist groups, whereas over the past decades (Islamic State and its affiliates aside) it has been the firepower of United Nations State Parties that has been overwhelmingly responsible for the devastation to material history—including but not limited to the United States, Russia, China, Israel and Saudi Arabia. Isis iconoclastically wrecked religious sites in Mosul, but it was the liberating forces that comprehensively flattened the historic city.

Looting, too, is problematically covered in the Paris exhibition. This is a serious issue in war zones where security vanishes. But the myth repeated here that the sale of looted artefacts is a meaningful source of terrorist funding “on a par” with resources such as oil is simply unevidenced. (Recovered Isis documents show something quite different.)

The exhibition is sponsored in part by the French office of Unesco. No surprise then that the organisation’s manifest failure to protect heritage in conflicts is absent from the walls. Unesco is celebrated—as it should be in some cases—for its work in Timbuktu, where the International Criminal Court brought the first (and, to date, only) successful prosecution for the targeting of monuments as a war crime. Less convincingly, the show argues that this episode was a turning point after which Unesco formulated a more grassroots approach to preserving culture by working with local people on local priorities.

It was Unesco that disgracefully praised Putin for liberating Palmyra despite the terrible damage Russian forces allied with Assad inflicted on Syria’s people and heritage. Unesco has been just as partial since: while it “strongly condemns” Russian attacks on heritage in Ukraine and Israel’s on Lebanon, it does not offer the same degree of pressure in its statements on heritage destruction in Gaza or Iran. Even then, unlike other UN agencies, Unesco never names Israel. Unesco has not invoked the 1954 Hague Convention in relation to Gaza, despite citing it in virtually all similar instances. Unesco did not seek urgent action by the UN Security Council or the General Assembly to protect cultural sites there as it did in respect of Isis.

The Paris show is more subtle in its understanding of the ways that post-war heritage reconstruction can be problematic and not necessarily healing, but is just as silent on Unesco’s move away from the centrality of authenticity to reconstruction work. Whereas the notion of rebuilding the Bamiyan Buddhas was deemed unacceptable, Unesco promoted building a brand-new Mostar Bridge in Bosnia and Herzegovina as peacebuilding—despite community relations actually deteriorating in the city. And then the agency had the temerity to declare the facsimile bridge a World Heritage Site, undermining its own scientific tenets to bolster a failed symbolic gesture. All this bad-faith is set out in my follow-up book, Monumental Lies (2022).

One is left to read between the lines for hints at the full curatorial mindset. Once through the exhibition doors, the first large-scale works displayed are photographs by the Palestinian artist Taysir Batniji of Gazans’ retrieved housekeys, with their heartbreakingly quotidian fobs—a friendship bracelet, a cheap carabiner clip, a Minnie Mouse figure. The unknown fate of their owners is pencilled in below.

In its silences and voids, Heritage in Resistance at least accurately mirrors failures of international institutions and laws and the partiality and misinformation that surrounds responses to contemporary heritage destruction. Ultimately, the show offers false hope about successful resistance via digital surveying, reconstruction and Unesco work. What we should be feeling is despair.

Enduring brand relevance with Gen Alpha means listening to what children want and how they want to feel and baking that into the core of the brand experience

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What unites the brands that kids love the most? Autonomy, discovery, sharing and collecting are recurrent themes, according to Beano Brain's 2026 Coolest Brands report.

Brands that resonate with Gen Alpha are often seen to be building affinity with the next generation of consumers. It's true that many connections formed with brands today will continue throughout adolescence and adulthood.

But the benefits of engaging Gen A audiences can often be seen sooner. Our Gen Alpha: Born to Shop research from earlier this year found that the UK’s 7-to 14-year-olds had £94 million worth of pocket money to spend on the high street.

Autonomy and self-discovery really matter to Gen Alpha, and we see this across some of the most popular brands that ranked in our research.

It’s no surprise when you consider that kids’ lives are still primarily spent following schedules and rules set by adults. Creating a space for them to explore their own interests gives them that freedom and ‘grown-up’ feeling.

YouTube – the number one coolest brand for the past three years – is a perfect example of this. The platform lets kids follow creators, explore new hobbies and move naturally between quick clips and long-form content. And importantly YouTube serves up content focussed on kids’ interests that simply isn’t available anywhere else – certainly not in traditional media.

The same is true of TikTok (#9), which also enters the top ten for the first time this year. But despite the apparent appeal of social media brands, even here kids are increasingly trying to gain control concerned with doomscrolling and other negative online experiences, 49% of 7-14-year-olds having actively taken time off social media; a third of those taking a break wanted more time for hobbies and interests.

Sign up to the design newsletter from Creative Bloq, brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of graphic design, branding, typography and more.

YouTube and TikTok are popular with younger audiences because they offer a chance for kids to explore and provide them with a sense of an owned space. But the important contradiction for brands to understand is that kids don’t want to spend all their time there and that sense of freedom isn’t limited to a screen.

Food, drink, and retail brands consistently score highly in our reports because they lead on innovation for example offering a range of limited-edition flavours and experiences for kids to explore. They’re also inherently shareable and must be experienced offline, - attributes of shareability and real-life experiences are loved by kids.

This is backed up by kids’ preferred shopping habits. In Gen Alpha: Born to Shop, more than two thirds (68%) of kids preferred real shops to shopping online, while 90% preferred shopping with someone.

Retail, and particularly QSRs, offer kids affordable spaces for kids and tweens to spend time with family or friends. This is one reason McDonald's has risen to number two, and why food and drink brands in general account for 29% of our Top 100; they offer the chance for shared real-life experiences kids crave.

The return of toys and physical play also came through strongly.

Analogue toys and collectables tap into kids' love of building, trading, and sharing physical items. LEGO (#6), another top ten brand, not only appeals to kids' creativity, but also, through partnerships, allows kids to collect different sets and get imaginative in a hands-on way.

Pokémon (#34) is another brand that’s ‘cool’ this year. Its cards and merchandise give it a collectible and shareable real-world presence to reinforce the online games and TV shows, properties that may have been the introduction to Pokémon for kids.

It is these shareable and collectable traits that play into the popularity of food and retail brands. For McDonalds, Happy Meal collaborations give children another reason to anticipate a visit, bringing familiar characters and collectable formats into the experience.

YouTube, LEGO, Pokémon, and McDonald's all share some of the same attributes of discovery, autonomy, shareability, and collectability. In this context, what may seem like ‘surprise’ inclusions in the list – the discount stores Home Bargains (#88) and B&M (#83) – make sense. ‘Coolness’ is not a trend; it’s embedded in your brand's personality and the brand experience.

The lesson is not that every brand needs a viral moment or partnership to be ‘cool’. It is that lasting relevance starts with listening to what children want to do and how they want to feel, rather than where to reach them.

Gen Alpha’s choices may still surprise us. But the motivations behind them should not.

Helenor is an award-winning researcher in the kids and family insights field. With over 30 years of experience in kids media, Helenor is an authority on kids, authoring one of the first white papers establishing key Gen Alpha behaviours.

Helenor designed and manages Beano Brain's unique ethnographic kids panel which means she has her ear to the ground when it comes to all things new and emerging. Her thorough knowledge means she has unrivalled knowledge about what drives kids and their parents, the rhythm of their lives and what they think is cool (or not).

#9035. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

Last medically reviewed on June 27, 2024

#9034. What Is Internet Cinema?

Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot, a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet.

During last June’s heat wave, I found myself standing outside an unassuming office building in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, baking in the sun’s glare. The Gallery, a nomadic curatorial platform, had set up an exhibition, titled “WeWork (oralmoral)”, in one of the building’s vacant office spaces. In celebration of the show’s closing the curators were screening films, some of which fall into the category of what is being called “internet cinema,” a burgeoning movement, or method, that has been in the making since late 2020. Related Articles Using the Graphics of GTA, Sara Sadik Explores the Challenges France's Muslim Youth Face 'Desiring Machines' Dares Us to Imagine a Healthy Relationship with Technology

Once inside, I wandered around the cool, unlit space, laughing at funny paintings and sculptures until it was time to find a spot on the floor for the screening. Someone in front of me was hastily scrawling the lineup of the screenings on paper with a black marker and passing them around as fast as he produced them. One passed back to me. The first film on the list was Zarina Nares’ I am going to die (this is my sign) (2025). The projector was fiddled with and a rectangle of white with a buffer symbol appeared on the blank wall in front of the seated crowd.

A chorus of female voices rose up, all in some general distress, and while I couldn’t see these women, by the tone, I could tell they were speaking into a front-facing camera. The chorus cut out to a single voice, which spoke over dashcam footage of a car crash: “You’re having problems at work, your boyfriend broke up with you, your parents are mad at you, everything is going wrong, your car broke down – that is a good sign. Like, that is the very best sign.”What followed was a montage of TikTok videos featuring motivational advice. One video bled into another, linked by the formulaic hooks used by podcast bros, emotional car seat influencers, clips of celebrities’ acceptance speeches, athletes in interviews, or passionate pastors, all of which was set to music. One after another these TikToks reveal ‘the one thing that you need to learn’ in a high-speed carousel of intense emotion that feels increasingly forced as it becomes clear how many of these impassioned speeches are copies of one another.

“Internet cinema isn’t necessarily about the internet or its aesthetic but about its logic, how it functions and how it makes us feel,” Zarina Nares said in a phone call. On the process of making I am going to die, she added that “Clearly, I watched enough advice videos for too long that I kept getting more. Once you watch so many you see the formula behind them, whether it’s a certain cadence of speaking or certain music.”

Internet cinema was first defined in a 2007 paper by Chuck Tryon titled “New Media Studies and the New Internet Cinema.” The technologies and formats that concerned Tryon —iPods and camera phones, software like Final Cut Pro, and home movies—are far dated, but his paper was prescient, having tapped into impulses and concerns that reflect contemporary internet cinema: a do-it-yourself ethos that blurs the line between amateur and artist; the popularization of “niche exhibition;” and a “self-reflexive style” that works “to call attention to the narrative codes and technological specs that shape cultural productions.”

Contemporary internet cinema has its roots in the COVID-era, which saw an explosion of participation in internet culture and production, that often bled out into one particular place: Dimes Square, a patch of Manhattan where Chinatown and the Lower East Side meet.

One of the most memorable dramas that played out at the time was puppeteered by a then-anonymous internet figure who went by the name Angelicism01. This figure posted creeds about extinction on Substack, and gained infamy for growing a cult-like following among young women in New York (who had never met him). With the help of various film makers, he made a three-hour long movie called Film01 which includes fast paced montages of memes, tweets, videos of natural disasters and terrorist attacks, alongside long scenes featuring the ‘it-girls’ he had recruited. Writer Madeline Cash described Film01 in the art publication Spike as “an unsophisticated collage of localized content that mimics, rather than intervenes or questions, our digital conditions,” which ultimately did nothing more than tap “into the scene’s libidinal narcissism.”Yet, with some distance, Film01 has proven to be a productive experiment. One of Angelicism01’s collaborators, the filmmaker Dana Dawud, found internet footage to splice into the film, created short edits that became a part of the larger film, and remotely directed certain sequences. Dawud would go on to launch Open Secret, an international screening series of internet cinema that has since played a large part in consolidating disconnected artists and practices under the term.At the same time that young women were running around Dimes Square at Angelicism01’s request, people were locked away at home with TikTok. More than ever, people around the world were subjecting themselves to hours and hours of scrolling on this relatively new video content platform.“When you’re doom scrolling, there is, technically speaking, no specific author to this montage that you’re watching. So, it’s as if you’re exposed to radical experimental cinema all the time by a completely cynical industrial apparatus,” said 0nty, the co-author of “Dialogues on CoreCore & the Contemporary Online Avant-Garde” during a Zoom interview also attended by his co-author Mischa Dols. “The question is, how do you even begin to think about this problem? And I think internet cinema is an answer,” 0nty said.0nty and Dols describe internet cinema as a method, rather than a genre or an aesthetic, which seeks to expose or comment on the way that the internet functions through editing found footage.It’s worth noting that some works under the umbrella of internet cinema do feature the production of new images. Dahlia Bloomstone’s 20,000 Tokens (2025) is a screen recording of the artist chatting with men and exposing herself on the webcam site Chaturbate (the video is spliced with a glitching 3D-rendering of a blonde avatar in a black void). For The Sight is a Wound (2024), Parham Ghalamdar filmed himself burning his own paintings, as a statement on how tthe seemingly endless documentation of the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza has made images useless. Yet the particular process of editing found footage is usually highlighted in definitions of internet cinema because this method represents the folk practice that preceded internet cinema: corecore.

Core, or rather, -core, is a suffix that denotes some kind of bundle of aesthetics and moods. Cottagecore, for example, is a reference to an image universe of milkmaid tops, galoshes, a straw basket full of wildflowers, a shingled cottage, butter made with wooden tools, but also, beyond images, a wish for simple, optimistic, pastoral life. But corecore emerged not as a specific aesthetic but as a way of making video content through editing together music, clips from movies, podcasts, and other TikToks.These videos are often melancholic ruminations of the deep and unrecognized suffering of young men, the terrible sublimity of being alone with your screen, an alienated awareness of hurtling towards extinction while scrolling on your parents’ sofa. Watching compilations of corecore I reminded me intensely of my time on Tumblr as a teenager.

On Tumblr, the practice of posting and reblogging images, fragments of text, and GIFs under an “aesthetic” was a way of cultivating and nurturing a feeling: a world of images that created a visual language for all that we thought life could be. Painful, dramatic love; intensity chased by the doom of its own ephemerality; cold, beautiful suffering. In the pivot to video platforms, corecore takes that tendency to collect images and feelings and turns it into a form much more contained and shareable than a blog: the film.

Removed from the usual logics of personal branding and sponsorship deals, it became an exciting trend for those who take internet-based cultural production seriously. Corecore, as a mass movement of people making films on the same devices they watch them on, represented the realization of an old dream of experimental cinema: film as a truly collective practice.“Authorship gets really muddy, you have content creators and video artists making films on the same platforms. Dana [Dawud] has compared internet cinema to the way that SoundCloud functions, where people can steal your edit, steal your beat, steal a sample, and then it gets lost who put it online first, and that’s okay,” said Edison Niebla Rodriguez, a curator who also creates video art with his wife, Dayana Matasheva, under the name Demon Lovers Inc. “Obviously, it’s kind of at odds with video art which is very hard for people to see because of the way that the art market functions.”

That said, video art has been a major inspiration for artists working in internet cinema. Arthur Jafa’s Love Is the Message, the Message Is Death (2016) in particular is often cited as a kind of totem of legitimacy for internet cinema. The film is a montage of civil rights–era footage and grainy videos of Black Americans circulated online: reaction memes, women twerking, women getting slammed to the ground by police, men getting shot by police, arms raised in the air. It’s profound love and profound despair, but also a comment on how images of Black people circulate online. When I first saw it, I was struck by how internet it felt: the video was playing on a laptop, which had been filmed by a phone camera. Of course, it turned out I’d been watching a bootleg, and that extra frame wasn’t part of the original.

Dawud’s film Palcorecore (2024) can be read in Jafa’s lineage. Like Jafa, Dawud cuts together found footage in an act of memory, love, and grief. The footage shows Palestinians flying kites, breakdancing, rapping, riding horses, and playing by the sea. Children surround a tank; a mute man desperately mimes a murder he witnessed. “The internet exists to document its own martyrdom,” a computerized voice says, playing on the fact that the Arabic word for martyr comes from the root meaning “to witness.” “We are martyrs together,” the voice says: we are witnesses together.“What interests me about internet cinema is that it creates a history of internet artists, the thoughts and languages they develop online, and the possibility of establishing a continuity between what they produce on the internet and how it can be given a temporal form through cinema,” wrote Dawud in an email. “Internet cinema doesn’t merely document an existing culture; it participates in the creation of its history. It is a way for the internet to historicize itself.”Ultimately, internet cinema is less a practice than a name: one that gives form to a whole range of ways of making online that are often lost in the tumult of the internet’s incessant production. If there is one thing that separates the art world from online cultural production, it is that the art world is nothing if not a form of memory. In its obsession with provenance, catalogues, and archives, it is a network of stewardship. Internet cinema is a means of making an object of what is so fleeting online, by turning the internet into a film.

#9032. Warhol’s Watches

Piaget’s second collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts translates the pop artist’s 1986 Camouflage self-portraits into dials made of gemstone marquetry.

One brand, however, stood out. Warhol owned at least seven wristwatches by the Swiss maison, Piaget. Founded in 1874 in La Côte-aux-Fées, a village in the heart of Switzerland’s Jura mountain range, the house was renowned in the latter half of the 20th century for its creative selection of timepieces in unusual shapes, many featuring dials made of exotic ornamental stones. One of those watches, a quartz-powered reference 15102 model that Warhol purchased from the brand in 1973, now forms the foundation for a Piaget collection bound to appeal to lovers of art in general and fans of Warhol’s revolutionary oeuvre in particular.

Housed in an 18-karat gold, 45 mm cushion-shaped case designed by Jean-Claude Gueit, Piaget’s then artistic director, the striking piece, which was part of a limited series manufactured between 1972 and 1977, featured a black onyx dial. Fittingly, it was called the Black Tie. In 1988, Piaget purchased Warhol’s watch at Sotheby’s landmark sale.

The artist’s choice of Piaget was no accident. In the 1950s and ’60s, the house had built its reputation on extreme thinness, introducing ultra-thin movements that transformed the watches into slim, supple pieces of jewelry. By the 1960s, Piaget had paired that technical prowess with a bolder sensibility: gold bracelets, vivid hardstone dials, and silhouettes that owed more to the jeweler’s bench than to the watchmaker’s. The result was a crossover brand that suited the decade’s appetite for spectacle. For Warhol, who drew no line between commerce and art, a watch that doubled as a gem-set object was irresistible. The Black Tie’s onyx dial, as sleek and dark as a lacquered cigarette case, could not have been better suited to the man who documented the era’s elite so closely.

Twenty-six years after Piaget purchased the Black Tie, the brand used the occasion of its 140th anniversary in 2014 to create a revival collection called Black Tie Vintage. The line caused such a stir among Piaget’s clientele that in 2024, for its sesquicentennial, the maison decided to up the ante. Thanks to a collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Piaget was given the rights to rename the Black Tie Vintage watch after Warhol himself.

The first collaborative watch to emerge from Piaget’s work with the foundation was the 2025 Collage, a limited edition of 50 pieces featuring an artful composition of ornamental stones—yellow Namibian serpentine, pink opal, and green chrysoprase—inspired by Warhol’s Polaroids. This month, Piaget has introduced a second piece, which also uses ornamental stone marquetry, this time to pay tribute to the Camouflage self-portraits that Warhol created in 1986.

“When you buy it, you don’t only buy a watch, you buy a whole story and heritage,” Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s head of patrimony, tells ARTnews. “You can, of course, talk about the material, what it does for you. But at the same time, you have to talk about Warhol, you have to talk about Piaget, you have to talk about art.”

Limited to 86 pieces, after the year in which Warhol created the eight-print Camouflage series, the watch, whose dial combines the ornamental stones sodalite and turquoise with satin-finished yellow gold and polished rose gold, faithfully interprets the artist’s work without blindly mimicking it.

“Camouflage is very difficult to work on, even in design, because we don’t just copy and paste the artwork—we have to find another way to express camouflage,” Forot says.

Among the final serial group of paintings Warhol completed before his untimely death in 1987, the works paid homage to the military-inspired camouflage pattern, originally intended to help soldiers blend in with their surroundings. In Warhol’s hands, they became a comment on Abstract Expressionism, not to mention a deeply personal statement on his lifelong effort to conceal his true self beneath wigs, makeup, and a carefully constructed facade.

Printed in acid brights across enormous canvases, the swirling forms feature in self-portraits overlayed with Warhol’s face, framed by his signature shock of hair. For an artist who spent his life hiding in plain sight, the Camouflage series is arguably his most meta work.

In order to capture the essence of the paintings on the face of a watch, Piaget’s artisans took some liberties with color. Rather than emphasizing Warhol’s use of yellow, for example, they highlighted the brand’s use of turquoise, Forot says.

“Once the team finished the drawing, which was validated by The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, then they started working with the gem material,” he says. “We have to try to remain true to both the design itself as well as the techniques.”

Study the dial of the watch and you’ll see something of an optical illusion: a sense of depth and texture that isn’t quite there. “When you look at the Piaget Camouflage, you have the feeling that you have four layers,” Forot says. “But in fact, it’s an illusion because they are all flat and on the same level. Even if you have the feeling that the turquoise is above the gold, in fact, it’s at the same level.”

The careful craftsmanship required to make the watch—each dial features 27 pieces of gold and ornamental stone marquetry and takes more than 100 hours of labor to design, research, and craft—is a testament to Piaget’s decades of expertise in the esoteric world of gem-setting. Since the maison introduced gold and color into its watches in the 1960s, it has worked with some 50 different ornamental stones, including lapis lazuli, jade, coral, onyx, and tiger’s eye.

The maison’s legitimacy in the realm of color is unassailable—and enduring. Piaget designated 2026 its “Year of Color,” based on its Colours of Extraleganza collection, representing the third and final chapter of a high jewelry trilogy that began with the maison’s 150th anniversary in 2024. “Piaget is really coming back to visibility in color and gold,” Forot says.

While the blend of hues on the dial of the Camouflage watch lends the piece its name and raison d’être, don’t overlook its iconic gold frame nor the movement that ticks within. The cushion-shaped case features three rows of textured grooves known as gadroons, a Piaget signature. It houses a self-winding manufacture movement, the 501 P1. And let’s not forget the caseback, where Andy Warhol’s signature appears alongside the number of timepieces in the limited series.

Best of all, the Camouflage limited edition, like the Collage that came before it, is steeped in the lore that swirls around Warhol’s personal history with Piaget.

“Warhol was a real collector—of everything,” Forot says. “But even if he owned many watches from many brands—including Patek Philippe, Cartier, Bulgari, and so on—there is only one picture with him and the founder of a watchmaking company. And it’s Yves Piaget.”

The legendary chairman of the maison, Yves Piaget is the fourth generation of his family to be involved in the business, which was founded by Georges-Édouard Piaget in 1874 and acquired by the Swiss luxury group Richemont in 1988. In the 1970s, at the height of the brand’s 20th-century popularity, Yves and Warhol became friends.

A photo of the men dated 1979 offers proof that they found common ground in their shared love of timepieces. At the time, Yves presided over the Piaget Society, a glamorous social circle centered on the brand and its community of jet-setting movers and shakers. And Warhol, of course, had the Factory, his studio in Manhattan, a hub of art, filmmaking, and creativity.

“They weren’t exactly the same, but they were both surrounded by artists, extravagant personalities—they were social long before The Social Network,” Forot says. “In a sense, they had the same philosophy.”

Yves’ recollections of Warhol during that time paint the artist as a quiet figure, whose later fame didn’t square with his penchant for careful observation.

Nevertheless, the two hit it off. Yves invited Warhol to Palm Beach to attend the world cup of polo, a sport that the maison made famous through its 1979 Polo timepiece, an emblem of the rich and famous. And he continued to send Warhol gifts, including boxes of chocolate, that the artist, a true magpie, kept as part of his time capsules. Stored in cardboard boxes, the objects, ephemera, letters, and gifts Warhol collected included personal relics from his multiyear friendship with Yves, although Forot jokes that the box of chocolate, while part of the collection housed by The Andy Warhol Museum in Pittsburgh, is, thankfully, empty.

Warhol’s attraction to the brand was hardly anomalous. Piaget’s clientele included more than its fair share of the rich and famous, including Jackie O, Elizabeth Taylor, and Halston. Even Salvador Dalí was a longtime collaborator. In 1967 the surrealist teamed with Piaget on a collaborative collection of gold watches and jewelry, long before such partnerships became commonplace. Featuring gold coins, dubbed Dali D’Or, emblazoned with profile portraits of himself and his wife, Gala, the watches and jewels that emerged from the partnership offer yet another testament to Piaget’s high-flying reputation as the watch for those in the know and a symbol of wealth, taste, and extravagance, all qualities that continue to define the brand today.

Michael Dayton Hermann, managing director of strategic initiatives at The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, says that the collaboration with Piaget “is an expression of how the artist’s vision remains as relevant and compelling today as ever.”

“This unique ongoing project is especially meaningful given Warhol’s personal friendship with Yves Piaget and his passion for the maison’s watches, which he collected during his lifetime,” Hermann tells ARTnews. “It also embodies Warhol’s belief in the creative possibilities of art and commerce, generating proceeds that support the foundation’s philanthropic mission, which has awarded more than $300 million in grants to advance contemporary visual art.”

Just as the collaboration celebrates Warhol’s singular take on the role art plays in commerce, it equally underscores Piaget’s decades-old legitimacy in the world of art. Watches may not be the first things that come to mind when recalling Warhol and his legacy, but he collected them, wore them, and, in the case of Piaget, befriended the man who made them. Think of the Camouflage limited edition less as a commercial arrangement and more as the next chapter of a decades-long conversation started by Warhol and carried on in gold and gems.

#9031. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

#9030. An archaeological take on ancient rituals in the heart of a legendary Berlin nightclub

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, A Shroud Woven of Solar Threads, 2026. Installation view at Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe

Press any key to continue is a monthly column about the ways technology is reshaping contemporary art, from non-fungible tokens and artificial intelligence to attention economies and new systems of distribution. Its author, Sarp Kerem Yavuz, is a visual artist, researcher and the artistic director of the Contemporary Istanbul Foundation.

“The world is changed. I feel it in the water. I feel it in the earth. I smell it in the air. Much that once was is lost, for none now live who remember it.” Cate Blanchett, as the high elf Galadriel, spoke these opening lines in The Fellowship of the Ring (2001), and in darkened cinemas around the world, her delivery set the tone for the wonder that followed. Not since my first viewing of that film 25 years ago had I felt that sense of being dwarfed by mythology, and to re-experience it in Berlin’s famous nightclub Berghain of all places was a delight.

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, an artist duo hailing from Iran and Canada, respectively, expertly blended archaeology, artificial intelligence (AI), acoustics, chemistry and sculpture to create a profoundly multi-sensory experience in A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads earlier this autumn (2-18 October).

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, Sūryasya Śántau (Within the Solar Silence), 2026. Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe

Situated inside Halle am Berghain—a gargantuan former power station that, yes, was reminiscent of J.R.R. Tolkien’s Khazad-dûm—the installation was presented by the Berlin-based contemporary art initiative House, helmed by Juliet Kothe, who co-curated with Nadim Samman. The exhibition was co-presented by the Autotelic Foundation, whose whimsical take on AI art in Venice had been one of the standout digital presentations during the most recent Biennale.

At the centre of A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads was a towering, eight-minute-long, 4K video installation that slowly panned through a digitally rendered, 4,000-year-old Mithraic cave temple, created based on 3D scans of the ancient site. Originally made for an exhibition in Lausanne in 2025, the installation was expanded to take advantage of the Halle am Berghain’s size.

As the “camera” floated through the ancient temple in the looping video, visitors were encouraged to position themselves in the center of the installation, where they would be encircled by human-height black monolithic speakers. Each speaker featured a different voice, all chanting in an AI-generated, speculative Proto-Indo-Iranian (PII). PII is the ancestor of the Indo-Aryan and Iranian language families, including Sanskrit and Avestan. There are no historic documents or written texts in PII, let alone documented Mithraic chants from that period.

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, A Shroud Woven of Solar Threads, 2026. Installation view, Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe

To realise the vital sonic component of the installation, the artists worked with the University of Toronto, drawing on comparative linguistics to reconstruct plausible linguistic forms. AI then allowed them to bring the speculative language to life. One of the speakers, Roushan said, was based on her own mother’s voice, which had been used to train one of the AI chanters.

"Mithra…" the chant began, referring to the ancient solar deity, a kind of lesser-known Ra, and as the incense burning in the hall filled one’s nostrils it was difficult not to feel transported by the sheer scale and the acoustic prowess of the installation. Near the ceiling, graffiti of the Eye of Horus that pre-dated the exhibition oddly contributed to the compounding of ritualistic symbols that have accumulated in the hall.

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, To Have a Shell is to Surrender, 2026. Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe

There is an inherent futility in worshipping an ancient sun god for any kind of wish-fulfillment. But ritualistic production and devotion have persisted through millennia and in our lives today, be it in our fascination with our illuminated, hand-held screens, or our commitment to attend public dance events that encourage abandon—such as the one that took place the weekend of Roushan and Stankievech’s opening, several metres and a few layers of concrete away. Objects scattered throughout the exhibition space included replicas of Bronze Age bells and reliefs, objects of ritual and religious significance that adorned the space and further contextualised the spiritual dimension of the installation, although none so potent as the ever-burning incense.

“We are all subject to digital change in society, economy, politics,” Nadim Samman, the Autotelic Foundation’s director, says. “These changes are massive, they are abrupt and they are intense. Making sense of it needs to come from below. Artists offer important ways to understand what this change means. Without artists, we are just stuck with the narratives and the images supplied by the companies that make the technology. Digital change impacts culture, and artists can help us understand what that impact actually feels like, and how we can think it through."

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, The Most Naked Thing in Existence, 2026. Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe

Since we have no recordings of PII, it is hard to refute that AI contributed a vital component of the installation. The exhibition’s thoughtful and archaeological approach to incorporating technologies that help us to speculate on the past was a welcome counterpoint to many digital art exhibitions in recent memory.

Roushan and Stankievech’s ambitious undertaking stands as one of the highlights of what has been a busy year for digital and AI-generated artistic presentations. The rather romantic gesture of leveraging AI to take us back several thousand years, to a time of fascination with nature and solar worship, and the decision to do so within the Brutalist context of a power-station-cum-nightclub, cleverly brought together many disparate threads.

“Studio Berlin” offers a way to circumvent the toughest door policy in the world and see works by Olafur Eliasson, Wolfgang Tillmans and Anne Imhof

A lacklustre show begs the question: can Holzer survive the scrutiny that her institutional exaltation invites in 2024?

Both AI-generated art and digital art have had a tough time lately, but the 61st Venice Biennale offers the digitally-minded some work to feel good about

#9029. London’s New Museum Needs a Better Reason to Exist

The new London Museum has been a humongous undertaking: 10 years in the making, costing £437 million in total against a budget of £337 million, and yet, after all that time and money, it’s hard to know where any of it went.

From 1976 to 2022, the city’s museum, then called the Museum of London, occupied a site on London Wall at next to the Barbican complex. It moved to Farringdon, a grittier neighbor of the City’s financial district, because the old building was hard for visitors to find and too small to display the full collection. Related Articles Bloomberg Donates 14,000 Artifacts Unearthed in Renovation to London Museum Warhol's Watches

The new space is bright and airy, closer to an Erewhon café than a museum lobby. An on-site café, open around the clock from Thursday to Sunday, serves hot chocolate and ginger beer. The furnishings, though, feel random in such a pristine setting: a flock of large plastic sheep meant for sitting on, and shop signs from London fixtures like the Odeon cinema and Morley’s, the fried chicken chain. When was the last time any Londoner saw a sheep in the city? In theory, all of this should appeal to Londoners who have taken up early-morning run clubs, traded pints for matcha lattes and aren’t above a gimmicky bit of decor.

“People are looking for community, and they will have it in the museum,” Sharon Ament, the museum’s director, told ARTnews.

The architects, Asif Khan and Stanton Williams, working with the conservation specialists Julian Harrap Architects, have designed a space that’s inviting.

“It took people until the 21st century to realize that cultural institutions are for everyone, and that’s what we strive to make here,” Khan told ARTnews at the press preview. He wants visitors to dip in and out of the story of London without feeling as if they’re in a museum. “When we look at audiences outside of the regular museum visitors, many find it challenging and don’t feel welcome. This is a welcome for those people,” Khan said. Entry is free, there are three separate entrances, and built-in sofas with reading lights invite passersby to stop in, though few people pass through Farringdon unless they’re waiting for the nightclub Fabric or the cocktail bar Space Talk to open.

Still, London is a city of 9.1 million people and a global center for art, film, music, finance and fashion. Finding stories that capture its quirks shouldn’t be that hard.

The museum is divided into three sections. Real Time, at the main entrance, represents London today and includes Banksy’s Piranhas sentry box. (What could be more London than Banksy?) In the Linbury Hall, Our Time attempts to tie the city together through objects like the Lord Mayor’s State Coach from 1757, the Buckingham Palace switchboard and Syd’s Coffee Stall, an East End food cart that operated from 1919 to 2019. Downstairs is Past Time, perhaps the only part of the museum that feels like a museum. It’s the most educational section, with small rooms on the women’s suffrage movement and the Great Fire of London. The rest of the floor is scattered with a piece of a fatberg, Tom Daley’s diving trunks from the London 2012 Olympics, a chair owned by Charles Dickens, a 2,000-year-old Roman wall painting, Anna Pavlova’s tutu for The Dying Swan and more.

The London Museum is a work in progress and until it figures out what sets it apart from the city’s other museums, it will remain a large crèche, where parents can bring their children to roam freely. But there’s still some hope: in 2028, the museum will open two temporary exhibition spaces, perhaps the museum will finally lean into its London-ness and celebrate the cornerstones that makes the city so glamorous and gritty, from the Teddy Boys of 1950s, Mods and Rockers of the 1960s to the Sloane Rangers of the late 1970s and 1980s.

Until the London Museum gets it right, the city has the Bayeux Tapestry, on view at the British Museum through July 11, 2027, with tickets topping out at £33 ($44). At the preview, word went around that one journalist had skipped it in favor of the 950-year-old cloth. In hindsight, I should have done the same, or stayed home to play Grand Theft Auto VI.
