Picture this: you're stepping off a direct overnight flight at Dublin Airport, passport in hand, ready to spend two weeks exploring Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way — and the transatlantic crossing that would have cost you $600 per seat cost you just 13,000 Avios instead. That's the moment this redemption delivers. For the ChooseFI community, the math here is almost offensive in how good it is. A round-trip economy ticket from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus typically runs $300–$600 per person, and during peak summer travel it can climb even higher. At 13,000 Avios one-way, you're squeezing **2.3 to 4.6 cents per point** out of every Avios you redeem. To put that in perspective, most loyalty program analysts consider 1.5 cents per point a solid redemption. You're potentially tripling that benchmark on what is genuinely one of the easiest award bookings in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The pricing inefficiency here runs deep. British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart** — meaning the price in Avios is determined by how many miles the plane physically flies, not by what the airline thinks the market will bear on that route. The North Atlantic crossing from the U.S. East Coast to Ireland is, by aviation standards, a relatively short haul. Dublin sits closer to Boston than Los Angeles does. That geographic reality, baked into BA's award chart structure, means you pay a "short-haul" price for what most travelers consider a major international trip. Aer Lingus operates modern Airbus A321LR aircraft on these transatlantic routes — a genuine premium product in economy with dedicated transatlantic seating, meal service, and that unmistakably warm Irish hospitality. This isn't a cramped regional jet. You're flying a purpose-built transatlantic cabin at a fraction of the cash cost. For a family of four, this redemption is transformational. At 13,000 Avios per person each way, a family round trip costs 104,000 Avios total — a points balance that's achievable with a single well-timed credit card welcome bonus. The alternative? Dropping $2,400 or more in cash for the same four seats. That's real money that stays in your FI journey.

The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. The ChooseFI community travels smart: avoiding peak summer crowds and booking shoulder seasons isn't just about lower prices, it's about a better experience overall.

Avios are accessible from virtually every major transferable points currency:

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Bilt mean you can search for availability, confirm your seats, then transfer points — no need to speculatively move points weeks in advance. That flexibility is a significant advantage for planning.

One important program nuance: Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. As long as you earn or redeem at least once every three years, your balance stays alive. For most ChooseFI members who hold a Chase or Amex card and regularly earn points, this is a non-issue — but it's worth knowing before you let a balance sit dormant.

Before transferring a single point, verify that award space actually exists on your target dates. Navigate to aerlingus.com and search for flights on your route (Boston, New York JFK, or Chicago ORD to Dublin). Aer Lingus displays Avios availability directly on their website — look for the "Avios" fare option when selecting your flight. This is the cleanest way to confirm seats before committing your points.

Alternatively, log into your British Airways Executive Club account at ba.com and use their award search tool. Search for Aer Lingus flights between your U.S. city and Dublin. The results will show Avios pricing — what you're looking for is the off-peak rate, which will display as lower Avios than the standard/peak option.

Use the BA award calendar view to spot off-peak pricing. Generally, traveling outside of peak summer (late June through August) and major holidays will unlock the best Avios rates. Shoulder seasons — late September through November and February through mid-April — are where the ChooseFI community finds the sweet spot of lower crowds, lower prices, and still-beautiful Irish weather.

Once you've confirmed availability on your target dates, calculate the total Avios needed: 13,000 per person, per direction. For a round trip for two, that's 52,000 Avios. Don't transfer until you're ready to book immediately.

Go to ba.com, log into your Executive Club account, and complete the award booking. This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

#9026. The Critic as Artist (And Vice Versa): A Fireside Chat with Jerry Saltz

During Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America, I had the great pleasure of doing a fireside chat with New York magazine senior art critic Jerry Saltz.

Like many of us, Jerry has been skeptical of AI, so I started the conversation by reading him a description of his approach to criticism produced by an AI that was based on a talk he gave a couple years ago. After chewing on that for a few minutes, we went on to speak about how he became a critic, how he became famous on social media, what he thinks about art being produced today, his strong feelings about auctions (he despises them), and what advice he would give creative people.

We also touched on the recent documentary made about Jerry and his wife, the former New York Times chief art critic Roberta Smith. And of course, it wouldn’t be a conversation with Jerry without plenty of engagement with the audience.

Despite its myriad challenges, Jerry still believes in New York City as a center for artists, and as a place with a vital community. You can watch the full talk, which took place on Saturday, November 14 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, via the video here.

#9025. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

#9023. Dead Man Is Accused of Stealing Art from Michigan Museums

The FBI is seeking a warrant to search electronic devices belonging to a Grand Rapids man accused of stealing art from two Michigan art museums. The news was reported by multiple outlets, including MLive.

According to a federal affidavit, Mikolai Augustine Stasiulewicz, 27, allegedly stole a color lithograph by artist Ellsworth Kelly, from Western Michigan University’s (WMU) Richmond Center for the Visual Arts on June 23. A worker notified WMU police that the work was missing, and Stasiulewicz, who was caught on surveillance video carrying the framed print, was identified through facial-recognition analysis by Michigan State Police. Related Articles 13th-Century Carving Stolen by Art Thief 'Eric the Belgian' Recovered in the UK Stolen Picasso Prints Found Under Pile of Clothes in French Riviera Apartment

Stasiulewicz is also alleged to have stolen a 16th-century Albrecht Dürer print from the Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM) on July 2. According to the FBI, he had been seen at the museum on June 17, “in what appeared to be a pre-theft surveillance visit.” Between the two thefts, he is accused of entering nonpublic areas at the Muskegon Museum of Art on June 25; however, Muskegon police said he didn’t take anything.

The FBI, which eventually took over the case, learned during its investigations that Stasiulewicz had met with a man on July 8 at the Gun Lake Casino Resort in Wayland, Michigan. Surveillance video shows him leaving with an unknown amount of cash.

Stasiulewicz was found dead in his home on July 30. According to the Kent County Medical Examiner’s Office, he died of a morphine overdose on July 26. Although the office’s autopsy report rules the death an accident, it also notes that “the decedent is currently under investigation by the FBI for involvement in an art gallery theft,” and that a brother had told police that may have played a part in his death.

Four artworks, including the Kelly, valued at $10,000 and the Dürer, valued at $10,000–$20,000, were found at the home the next day.

On Monday, November 23, the FBI sought a warrant to search Stasiulewicz’s cellphone and laptop computer to determine if any others were involved in the thefts. “In my training and experience, and that of the Art Crime Team, phones and computers like the devices will often be used to communicate with co-conspirators,” FBI Special Agent Evan Alkema wrote in the federal affidavit. “They may contain evidence of communications about what art pieces to steal, negotiations for sale prices, and arrangements to transfer and ‘fence’ the stolen works.”

Since its inception in 2004, the FBI’s Art Crime Team, which handles cases involving the theft, forgery, and trafficking of art and cultural artifacts, has recovered more than 20,000 objects valued at $1 billion.

Stasiulewicz was an amateur artist who studied at the Interlochen Center of the Arts, the FBI said.

#9022. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

#9021. Shigeru Ban unveils proposal for tent-like church in Rome

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects

A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.

The church will occupy a currently underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a “fragmented urban fabric”.

“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together,” said Ban.

“The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a new sense of belonging in the neighbourhood.”

Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci’s proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the New Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.

As part of the project, four new churches will be built, while one existing parish complex will be extended.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be built on a raised public plaza, with various parish facilities, community spaces and a priest’s residence embedded below.

Its key feature will be its angular roof, which is shaped like a cross but not immediately readable as one. This is modelled on a latent cross – a feature in sacred architecture, in which a cross shape is integrated in the spatial design, without being clearly visible.

Inside, the church will have a diamond-shaped plan, with large stained-glass windows positioned in the four cardinal directions. They will be triangular in shape and feature designs modelled on neighbourhood street art.

The project will be complete with a landscaped park, as well as various recreational and sports facilities, which the studios said will “create opportunities for social interaction and everyday activities”.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex is not the first church project by Ban. Among his others is the landmark Cardboard Cathedral in New Zealand, which is formed of 98 cardboard tubes combined with wood and polycarbonate. We named it the most significant building of 2013 in our list of the 25 most significant buildings of the 21st century.

Other Italian church proposals recently featured on Dezeen include Stefano Boeri Architetti’s design for the Ambrosian Monastery in Milan, which will have a sail-like roof form.

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects

CD Projekt Red says Rockstar's latest blockbuster has raised the bar for open-world visuals and design, but artists matter more than budgets.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 is having a wider impact than just being one of the highest-rated games ever, with a 99 on Metacritic; it’s making other developers rethink what they’re doing. This week, many devs came out and praised GTA 6’s technical achievements, from CD Projekt Red to Naughty Dog, but behind the scenes, those same creators are setting new benchmarks to complete.

The impact of GTA 6 is simple: it’s as impressive as all great art is, because it expands what's possible through a captivating vision and flawless execution. And it’s making developers think and rethink.

CD Projekt Red is no slouch when it comes to technically advanced games and graphics, but even they are having that moment. The studio behind The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 has admitted that GTA 6 inspires its developers, with joint CEO Michał Nowakowski saying he expects The Witcher 4 to make a similarly huge leap over its predecessor.

As reported on Polygon, speaking during the company's latest investor call, Nowakowski was asked whether the jump from The Witcher 3 to The Witcher 4 would be comparable to the one between GTA 5 and GTA 6. His answer was pretty emphatic.

"Do we believe there's going to be a comparable leap between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4? I think so, yes," he said. "I mean, it's been 11 years."

The studio is working to make The Witcher 4 "significantly better-looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game", adding that players should expect a much bigger jump between the two games.

That's quite a promise, although there's a good reason to be ambitious. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is now 11 years old, and while its world still looks fantastic (especially after its recent remaster), the technology and expectations for open-world games have moved on considerably.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

GTA 6 is an obvious comparison, but I'm more interested in what CD Projekt Red does differently. Rockstar has its own way of building a world, and The Witcher's appeal has always been its atmosphere, character design, and strong writing. I don't need Ciri's world to look like Vice City, but I do want the same depth and sense of a living world Rockstar has created. Following this year’s Unreal Engine 5.6 tech demo, I’m sure The Witcher 4 will impress, possibly setting a new standard.

CD Projekt Red is clearly putting a lot of its development resources into The Witcher 4. Its latest figures show 513 developers working on the game, compared with 199 on Cyberpunk 2. The latter is still in the earlier stages of development, so expect that team to grow. The Witcher 4 is currently targeting a 2028 release, while Cyberpunk 2 is further away, and by that time we’ll be in the realms of PlayStation 6 and Unreal Engine 6.

There's also a question of how much money studios need to spend to reach these new visual standards. Nowakowski was keen to stress that GTA 6 hasn't changed CD Projekt Red's development philosophy, describing its projects as ambition-driven rather than simply budget-driven.

Perhaps that's where the GTA 6 hype is sidelined: few developers have Rockstar’s billion-dollar budgets, and no indie ever will, but CD Projekt Red has UE6 and faith in its artists, technicians, and writers. You still need artists with a clear idea of what they want to create, and developers who know how to bring that vision to life.

#9019. Shahzia Sikander Sculpture in St. Louis Generates Protests and Counterprotests

Executive Editor, ARTnews & Art in America

Activists against women’s right to choose in relation to their reproductive rights protested a sculpture by Shahzia Sikander in St. Louis this week, calling for the removal of the 18-foot-tall work titled Witness (2023).

As reported by St. Louis’s First Alert 4, protesters associating the sculpture with pro-choice abortion rights gathered outside the home base of Rung for Women, a nonprofit devoted to women’s career development that hosts it. As the organization describes itself on its website, “Too many women are unfulfilled, unhappy, and underpaid in their jobs, but afraid to take the leap into the unknown. We designed a program to guide motivated women through a process to start working in exciting careers and get paid what they’re worth.” Related Articles Shahzia Sikander's Animated Film Selected for M+ Facade Commission in Hong Kong Shahzia Sikander Says She Won't Repair Beheaded Sculpture in Texas: 'A Testament to Hatred'

First Alert 4 quoted an activist with a group called Students for Life America associating Sikander’s sculpture with the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. “Her skirt spells Hava, which is Eve, the first female rebel, to breathe life,” said Reagan Barklage, who related the work to the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. “It’s just, you do not need to kill your children in order to breathe life. That’s actually the exact opposite of what that means.”

She continued: “We’re alarmed that this is what they’re choosing to use to represent our city. We do not stand for these pro-abortion rights. And we’re trying to stand for women and true empowerment.”

A counterprotester thought otherwise. “We’re here because this organization that’s located on this block has every right to display whatever artwork they want on their own property,” said Leslie Zacks, who spoke of the protest in the context of a recently failed amendment that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban. “The reality of the situation is that the people in Missouri have twice had the opportunity to voice their preferences with regards to the abortion issue and have made it very, very clear with increasing majority where their preferences are.”

Rung for Women issued a statement saying the organization “respects the right of individuals to express their views about art, including those that differ from our own. We recognize that Witness has prompted strong reactions and respect the sincerely held beliefs of those who have expressed concern. We remain proud to host this work by Shahzia Sikander at Rung for Women.”

The same sculpture by Sikander was the subject of heated protest in Texas in 2024, when it was decried by a group that called it “satanic” before it was to go on view at the University of Houston. After an opening and artist talk related to the work were subsequently canceled, Sikander said, “Art should be about discourse and not censorship. Shame on those that silence artists.”

An attempt by ARTnews to reach the artist was not immediately successful.

#9018. Meet Swedish Girls, Sabine Marcelis’s pick for Dezeen's 20x20 project

Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

The duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.

The Big Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

“We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

“The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”

Humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.

“We got the idea when we launched the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.

“A professor from Beckmans called and said that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.

“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”

Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.

“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” said Bergh.

Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things. But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.

“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

“But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”

“Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”

The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.

“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” said Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.

“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most important thing,” she continued.

“Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”

“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

The hardest thing is to earn money. We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.

The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

“The hardest thing is to earn money,” said Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”

“You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”

When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” said Zachrisson.

“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”

The duo said funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.

“All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”

Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.

“It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” said Bergh. “We have plans for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”

“I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”

#9017. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

As revealed by Memeio above, the Vice City portal Easter egg is a wildly complex multi-step time-travel secret with some very subtle clues, including "a sound effect from Vice City" when you power up the radio tower in Key Lento and individual letters that spell out a Vice City cheat code. #9015. Fictional Project designs home in Kerala to feel "one with the landscape"

Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.

Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.

This led Fictional Project to pull the home’s built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home’s pared-back and open interiors.

“The residence is careful not to overpower, becoming one with the landscape,” the studio told Dezeen.

Interstitial Living is organised around a bedroom at its centre, which is housed within a cubic volume finished in cement plaster.

A small window in this bedroom overlooks a potted tree within a cut-out in the floor of the adjacent living room, which faces the yard to the west through a row of full-height windows above a built-in timber bench.

On the opposite side of the home, the kitchen overlooks the eastern yard through a row of windows above its countertops. Both these spaces are defined by the curving white-plastered ceilings overhead, which sweep down from the centre of the home.

“The scale of the residence allows for intimate working spaces in the kitchen and a welcoming living room, all accentuated by the dynamic nature of the roof. The other spaces negotiate the private/public nature of the indoors,” the studio explained.

“The concavity of the roof creates a visual connection to the outdoors, becoming a marker that emerges from within the site.”

“It breaks the rigidity of a traditional sloping roof, helping create fluid indoor spaces. Nothing here is built or conceived in isolation, but rather as interconnected systems,” it added.

The smaller first floor contains a second bedroom, bathroom and a study area, which overlook the living space below from a steel-framed landing and internal windows.

While the internal finishes were kept minimal, the exterior of the home and its boundary walls were built using terracotta-toned textured blocks, which the studio described as introducing a sense of “groundedness and warmth”.

Other dwellings in Kerala recently featured on Dezeen include a home by InLe Architects framed and shaded by two large mango trees and a farmhouse by Evolving Radical Aesthetics that is built into a hillside above a carved-out, open-air temple.

#9014. Tate Liverpool Plans Fall 2027 Reopening With Surrealism Survey

Tate Liverpool will reopen in fall 2027 after a £30 million transformation with the exhibition “Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds,” a nod to the museum’s inaugural Surrealist show in 1988.

The surrealism exhibition will run from fall 2027 to spring 2028 and include works by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray. According to Tate Liverpool, the show will also explore the “important role of surrealism in the history of theater and dance” through the movement’s major commissions for stage sets and costumes. Also on view will be Dorothea Tanning’s costume designs for the ballet The Witch, photographs of Sheila Legge performing as the “Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal” at the opening of the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London, and material from the archive of Ted Joans. Related Articles Meryl Streep Makes Big Donation to National Women's History Museum, Musée d'Orsay Receives Collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist Fan Paintings: Morning Links for March 19, 2026 Museum of Liverpool Evacuated by Phony Bomb Threat

“Surrealism invites us to see the world differently and what better way to reopen Tate Liverpool. This exhibition will spark imaginations, surprise visitors and reward curiosity, offering a fresh perspective on one of art’s most celebrated movements. It also brings a wonderful echo of the surrealist exhibition that opened our gallery in 1988, while taking visitors on an exciting new journey,” said Jemima Pyne, interim director of the Tate Liverpool, in a statement.

Tate Liverpool closed in October 2023 and was scheduled to reopen in 2025, but fundraising difficulties pushed the date back to 2027. The architecture firm 6a architects is redesigning the gallery’s home, an 1846 warehouse on the Royal Albert Dock, as part of a £35 million ($46.5 million) renovation.

#9013. L-Tyrosine Supplements: Benefits for Your Brain and Body

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

#9012. SHoP Architects designs Novak Djokovic-backed Miami supertall skyscraper

New York studio SHoP Architects has released designs for a ribbed supertall skyscraper in Miami, announced alongside the launch of a luxury brand for which Serbian tennis player Novak Djokovic is developing amenity facilities.

SHoP Architects, who are behind some of New York City’s tallest buildings, designed the 1,049-foot-tall (320-metre-tall) skyscraper around ATMA, a luxury brand being launched by hospitality operator Aman Group.

If completed at the stated height, it would be taller than the city’s current tallest skyscraper, and have the same projected height as the in-progress Waldorf Astoria Hotel & Residences Miami, which has been cited as the city’s future tallest.

The skyscraper will include a hotel, residences and a members’ club. According to Aman Group, ATMA’s “advanced wellness programming and world-class sport facilities” will be developed “exclusively” with Djokovic, who is credited as a global partner of the new brand.

Designs for the skyscraper itself show a ribbed form of balconied terraces organised around a central void that runs from the crown to the podium.

It is planned for Miami’s Brickell neighbourhood, and Aman Group said that the floor-to-ceiling windows of the skyscraper will merge the “futuristic architecture with the bay”.

Toronto-based interiors outfit Studio Paolo Ferrari has been chosen as the interiors lead on the project. It will include condos with one to five bedrooms, with six-bedroom penthouses pushed to the top of the skyscraper.

The structure will have setbacks at the upper floors, presumably to create more panoramic views for residences in the penthouses.

The ATMA concept is based around what Aman Group calls “performance-driven lifestyle”.

“Monolithic architecture meets biomorphic design, furniture is shaped naturally to the human form and ambience adjusts sensitively to residents’ and guests’ circadian rhythm,” said Aman Group.

Djokovic’s programme, meanwhile, will include a 120,000-square-foot spa and wellness centre.

“ATMA Miami will sit at the pinnacle of what performance living can achieve,” said Djokovic.

OKO Group and Oak Row Equities were announced as developers for the project.

SHoP Architects is no stranger to supertall luxury residences. It designed New York’s skinniest supertall skyscraper to have single-floor apartments on the city’s so-called Billionaires Row. It also designed the Brooklyn Tower, the tallest structure in the borough.

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

What $10,000 grows to at different rates over 30 years — the rate difference matters more than you think.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 6% annual return

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 8% annual return

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 10% annual return

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Future value (FV) is the projected worth of an investment at a specific point in the future, based on an assumed rate of growth. It answers the most practical question in investing: "If I invest this money today, what will it be worth in 10, 20, or 30 years?"

Future value calculations rest on compound interest — the principle that your returns earn their own returns over time. Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest "the eighth wonder of the world," and while the attribution is debatable, the math is not. The difference between simple interest (returns on your original investment only) and compound interest (returns on your investment plus accumulated returns) becomes enormous over long time horizons.

The basic future value formula for a lump sum investment is:

For example, $10,000 invested at 8% for 20 years:

FV = $10,000 x (1.08)^20 = $10,000 x 4.661 = $46,610

The table reveals two critical insights. First, small differences in return rates produce massive differences over long periods — $10,000 at 6% grows to $57,435 over 30 years, while the same amount at 10% grows to $174,494. That 4-percentage-point difference triples the outcome. Second, time is the dominant variable. At 8%, your money doubles roughly every 9 years — so 30 years gives you more than three doublings, turning $10,000 into over $100,000.

Most people do not invest a single lump sum and walk away. They invest regularly — monthly or per paycheck — over decades. The future value of a series of regular contributions uses a different formula called the future value of an annuity:

Where PMT is the periodic contribution, r is the periodic rate, and n is the total number of periods.

In practice, you do not need to calculate this by hand. The insight that matters is this: regular contributions are far more powerful than most people realize because each contribution starts its own compounding clock. Your first $500 contribution compounds for the full 30 years, while your 360th contribution (at month 360) compounds for just one month — but together they build wealth that dwarfs a single lump sum.

A person investing $500 per month at 8% for 30 years accumulates $745,180 — from total contributions of only $180,000. That means $565,180, or 76% of the final balance, came from compound returns rather than your own deposits. This is the engine of wealth building.

Every future value calculation should be done twice — once in nominal terms and once in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. The nominal return is the raw number your investments earn. The real return subtracts inflation, showing you what your money will actually buy.

Historically, the S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% nominally and 7% after inflation. The difference matters enormously over long periods:

That $1.13 million in nominal terms has the purchasing power of roughly $610,000 in today's dollars — still excellent, but nearly half less than the headline number suggests. When planning for FI, always use real returns (6-7%) rather than nominal returns (9-10%) to avoid overestimating what your portfolio will actually support in retirement spending.

The Rule of 72 is the simplest and most useful mental math tool in investing. Divide 72 by your annual rate of return to estimate how many years it takes for your investment to double:

This works in reverse too. If you want to know what rate of return you need to double your money in 15 years: 72 / 15 = 4.8%. The Rule of 72 is an approximation — it is most accurate for rates between 5% and 12% — but it is remarkably precise within that range and far faster than pulling out a calculator.

The FI community uses future value calculations as the backbone of retirement planning. The process works in three steps:

The table shows how starting balance and monthly contribution interact. Notice that increasing your monthly contribution from $1,500 to $2,500 (a $1,000 increase) with a $100,000 starting balance cuts 3.5 years off your time to $1 million. This is the savings rate lever in action — the amount you save each month matters more than any other variable you control.

A common question is whether it is better to invest a lump sum now or spread contributions over time (dollar-cost averaging). The math is clear: lump sum investing wins approximately two-thirds of the time because markets trend upward over the long term. However, dollar-cost averaging reduces the psychological risk of investing a large amount right before a downturn and provides a behavioral advantage that keeps many investors on track. For most FI-seekers, the question is academic — you invest each paycheck as it arrives because you do not have a large lump sum sitting on the sidelines.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

When projecting your portfolio growth for retirement planning, use real (inflation-adjusted) returns of 6-7% rather than nominal returns of 9-10%. A $1 million nominal balance in 30 years has the purchasing power of roughly $550,000 in today's dollars at 2% average inflation. Planning with real returns ensures you are targeting a portfolio that can actually support your desired spending level.

Track your actual spending for 3 months and annualize it. Multiply by 25 to get your FI number using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. If you spend $60,000 per year, your FI number is $1,500,000.

Add up all retirement accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), taxable brokerage accounts, and savings. Exclude home equity and non-liquid assets. This is your starting balance for the future value calculation.

Subtract your monthly spending from your monthly after-tax income. Include employer 401(k) match and any other automatic savings. This is your periodic contribution amount for the future value formula.

Use the future value of a lump sum plus annuity formula, or a simple online calculator, to project when your current balance plus monthly contributions will reach your FI number. Use 7% real return (after inflation) for conservative planning.

Test what happens if you increase contributions by $200/month, $500/month, or $1,000/month. Seeing the concrete impact of a savings rate increase — often shaving 2-5 years off your FI timeline — makes the trade-offs tangible and motivating.

For long-term stock market projections, use 7% for inflation-adjusted (real) returns or 10% for nominal returns based on the S&P 500 historical average. For a more conservative estimate, use 6% real. For bond-heavy portfolios, use 3-4% real. Always specify whether you are using nominal or real returns — mixing them up is one of the most common planning mistakes.

Future value calculations show what WOULD happen if returns were constant every year. In reality, markets fluctuate — you might earn 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Over 20-30 year periods, average returns tend to converge toward historical norms, making future value projections reasonably useful for planning. Treat them as directional estimates, not guarantees.

Future value asks: "What will $10,000 today be worth in 20 years?" Present value asks the reverse: "What is $50,000 in 20 years worth in today's dollars?" They use the same variables but in opposite directions. Present value is useful for evaluating whether a future payout (like a pension or annuity) is worth the cost today.

The Rule of 72 works for any compounding rate, including inflation. At 3% inflation, prices double every 24 years (72 / 3 = 24). This means $50,000 in annual spending today becomes $100,000 in 24 years in nominal terms — your purchasing power is halved if your income stays flat. This is why investing in assets that outpace inflation is essential.

For FI planning, future value is more intuitive — it tells you what your portfolio will grow to. However, the most practical approach is to calculate future value using real (after-inflation) returns. This effectively gives you a future value stated in today's purchasing power, which is what you actually need to know for spending planning.

In tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), your investments compound without tax drag, so the standard future value formula works directly. In taxable accounts, capital gains taxes, dividend taxes, and tax-loss harvesting all affect your real return. A rough adjustment is to reduce your assumed return by 0.5-1.0% for taxable accounts to account for ongoing tax drag.

Future value calculations are the most practical tool in the FI planner's toolkit. They turn abstract concepts like compound growth and savings rate into concrete dollar amounts and specific timelines. The key takeaways are straightforward: use 7% real returns for conservative planning, always account for inflation by using real rather than nominal returns, and remember that your monthly contribution rate has a far larger impact on the outcome than chasing an extra point or two of return. The Rule of 72 gives you instant mental math for any investment decision — how long to double, what rate you need, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. Combined with a clear FI number and a disciplined savings rate, future value projections show you exactly when financial independence becomes reality. Run the numbers, test different scenarios, and let the math motivate you to increase that monthly contribution whenever you can.

#9010. Smithsonian Head Assures Staff of Independence After Glimpse of White House Overhaul Plan

Outgoing Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III reasserted the institution’s independence in a letter to his staff after a leaked document from a Trump aide laid out a sweeping overhaul of its programming and personnel.

“The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in the letter, which the New York Times reviewed and first reported. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.” Related Articles Did a Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveal White House Plans to Revamp the Smithsonian? Rep. Jamie Raskin Wants the Smithsonian to Collect and Display Trump's Propaganda, To Teach About Tyranny

The document, titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan,” was photographed on a laptop that a Trump aide was using on the Washington Metro. As first reported by ProPublica, its 25-item action list includes plans to dismiss top curators and administrators, among them Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, whom the White House has accused of promoting “radical activist ideology.”

The plan also calls for a new permanent exhibit, “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance,” and another on “Great Families of American History.” It envisions a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington at the museum’s entrance, which would fulfill a request Trump made in September.

The plan appears to be a work in progress: Photos show the aide brainstorming additions in a notebook. One handwritten entry seems to read “No X-rated exhibition policy,” an apparent callback to a particularly contentious stretch of Hartig’s testimony, when lawmakers questioned her about images of bondage wear in an LGBTQ history exhibition. On Monday, ProPublica identified the staffer as an associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office behind a 162-page report that accused the Smithsonian of “extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.”

A central complaint of the report was what its authors characterized as anti-white bias at the museum, which they said showed in its promotion of diversity, equity, and inclusion. The report accused one exhibition, “Many Voices, One Nation,” of trying “to convince visitors that illegal aliens are entitled to citizenship, voting rights and ‘belonging’ in America.” (Two weeks after the report’s release, Trump signed an executive order directing that signs be installed outside the museum warning visitors of its “ideological capture.”)

The document glimpsed on the staffer’s laptop laid out new interpretive guidelines for exhibits, including an explicit end to the Smithsonian’s use of a diversity style guide. The Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions would be reviewed, and one show now on tour, “The Bias Inside Us,” would be halted. Grants to “woke third parties,” such as the American Alliance of Museums, would also be reviewed.

The Smithsonian’s online K-12 curriculum would be overhauled to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” The “Becoming US” module on immigration, for example, would be deleted and replaced with a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The Smithsonian, a network of 21 museums, is structured to operate independently of the White House. It’s governed by a 17-member Board of Regents: the Chief Justice of the United States, John G. Roberts Jr.; the Vice President, JD Vance; six members of Congress from both parties; and nine private citizens. Legally, the Smithsonian answers to Congress, not the White House, but federal money makes up about 60 percent of its budget. Trump proposed cutting that funding by roughly 12 percent for fiscal year 2026, a threat that ultimately went unrealized.

Bunch, who became secretary in 2019, has repeatedly asserted the institution’s legal independence as pressure from the White House has mounted. The administration has demanded that the Smithsonian turn over internal materials and pushed for the firing of Kim Sajet, the director of the National Portrait Gallery, whom Trump had called “highly partisan.” Sajet ultimately resigned. Bunch has drawn similar attacks: a White House aide reportedly called him a “rabid partisan.”

In a May interview with the New York Times, Bunch seemed to acknowledge that recent vacancies on the Board of Regents had weakened his position, though he still appeared to have the support of a majority of the board. In September, he announced that he would retire at the end of the year.

In his letter to staff on Tuesday, Bunch wrote, “As I have said before, we welcome scrutiny of our work, and even disagreement. The Smithsonian will continue to be driven by scholarship, research and reflection, free from outside influence and in service to the American people.”

#9009. Nip Slip? The Ultimate Guide to Inverted Nipples

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or issues with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

For some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

There are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

#9008. Sid Lee Architecture references "rhythm of the vine" for curved Ontario hotel

Photography by James Brittain (unless stated otherwise)

Canadian studio Sid Lee Architecture has created a curved-glass hotel that takes cues from the burgeoning wine region of Ontario.

The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel, a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

The rounded 94,000-square-foot (8,732-square metre) hotel sits on a property in the historic village that is being transformed by winemakers.

“The Clayfield was conceived as a new hub for Niagara-on-the-Lake, a place where wine culture and hospitality find a home,” Martin Leblanc, architect and co-founding partner of Sid Lee Architecture, told Dezeen.

“Its layered contours, rounded geometry and rhythmic wood elements translate the surrounding vineyard landscape into a building that celebrates the region’s contribution to Canadian winemaking.”

The hotel was conceived as a pavilion set in the emerging townscape between vineyards and the Clayfield Commons housing development on an agricultural road.

The curved form allows access and connection to its surroundings in multiple directions.

“The hotel acts as a threshold between these typologies, connecting the vineyard and the denser village-like development around it,” Leblanc said.

“Its exterior wood elements recall the rhythm of the vine rows, the layered concrete refers to the clay soil and the reflective glass registers the changing light, sky and seasons.”

The studio said that the organic, natural flow of a hotel is essential to the lasting success of the design.

Working back and forth between the architecture and the interior design, the studio laid out spaces to progress from public to private and back again, integrating moments for visitors to discover the landscape.

“As visitors approach and circulate around the building, it frames changing views of the vines, the plaza and the emerging neighbourhood,” Leblanc said. “The lobby acts as a gateway to the vineyard, while the rooftop terrace reconnects the hotel experience with its broader surroundings.”

Meanwhile, the staircase acts as a connector, transition and centrepiece between the plaza, lobby and upper levels.

“Inside, we chose a palette that speaks to the natural beauty of Niagara’s wine country: walnut panelling, concrete, dark amaranth-coloured leather, greige limestone and woven fabrics,” Leblanc said, calling out the limestone registration desk chiselled from the Niagara Escarpment and the restaurant’s curved bar that resembles the shape of the building.

With mostly Teknion furniture, each space represents a season of the vineyard, from spring in the lobby to winter in the guest rooms with more quiet, reserved furnishings that complete the rooms that fan out from the rounded concrete strata.

Founded in 2009, Sid Lee Architecture has six offices across North America and Europe. The studio previously remodelled its own offices in an I.M. Pei office building, overhauled the interiors of the iconic Fairmont Queen Elizabeth Hotel and created an artisan-inspired workplace for video game designers – all in Montreal.

We love a good optical illusion, and we've seen plenty of mind-benders over the years, but there's one really famous one that continues to intrigue scientists. The Müller-Lyer illusion looks so simple: two lines, one with arrows pointing inwards from the ends and one with arrows pointing out. One looks longer than the other, right?

A lot of people see it that way, but some people don't. Some people can immediately tell that the two horizontal lines are actually the same length (see below if you don't believe me). But the reason for this difference in perfection continues to be a topic of big debate.

This optical illusion was named after Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, its creator. Many people initially assume that the line with the arrows pointing inwards is longer than the other. But then research published in the 1960s claimed that people in African and Southeast Asian countries weren't so often fooled by the illusion. It seemed that WEIRD people were mode susceptible – that is, people whose backgrounds were Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and from a Democracy.

That led to a theory that the apparent difference might have something to do with people in industrialised societies being more exposed to sharp angles and straight lines when growing up, and that this somehow moulds their perception.

The problem is that the suggested difference in perception has now been called into question. As reported by Sciencing, Dorsa Amir and Chaz Firestone, anthropologists at Duke and John Hopkins, have gathered evidence opposing the theory developed in the 1960s and published their findings in the Psychological Review.

They note that many variation of the Müller-Lyer illusion have been developed, including ones that work in a similar way despite using curved lines instead of straight ones. Other similar illusions abound, including the Ebbinghaus illusion, in which two identical dots are perceived to be different sizes depending on whether they're surrounded by six large dots or eight small dots. In that case, there are no lines or angles at all.

Amir and Firestone also turned up flaws in the case studies from the 1960s, and found that later reports had misconstrued the original findings. The evidence that Africans and Asians aren't fooled by the Müller-Lyer illusion appeared to be very scant.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

But one discovery would seem to be even more conclusive in disproving the old WEIRD theory. The optical illusion has been tested on people who were born blind and later had lens replacement surgery, and it appears to trick people immediately after they gain sight despite them not having grown up seeing lines and angles around them.

With the WEIRD theory ruled out, it seems then that this old optical illusion has become weirder, becoming a mystery again
